claim: Deletion of BMAL1 in mice robustly increases expression of complement genes, including C4b and C3, in the hippocampus.
source: Here, we report that deletion of the master clock protein BMAL1 in mice robustly increases expression of complement genes, including C4b and C3, in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data from BMAL1 KO mice shown in Figure 1A and confirmed by qPCR in subsequent experiments.

claim: BMAL1 regulates expression of the transcriptional repressor REV-ERBα.
source: BMAL1 regulates expression of the transcriptional repressor REV-ERBα, and deletion of REV-ERBα causes increased expression of C4b transcript in neurons and astrocytes as well as C3 protein primarily in astrocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism and is supported by data showing REV-ERBα expression changes following BMAL1 deletion.

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα causes increased expression of C4b transcript in neurons and astrocytes.
source: BMAL1 regulates expression of the transcriptional repressor REV-ERBα, and deletion of REV-ERBα causes increased expression of C4b transcript in neurons and astrocytes as well as C3 protein primarily in astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from tissue-specific knockout mice shown in Figure 1B, 1C, and 1E.

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα causes increased C3 protein expression primarily in astrocytes.
source: BMAL1 regulates expression of the transcriptional repressor REV-ERBα, and deletion of REV-ERBα causes increased expression of C4b transcript in neurons and astrocytes as well as C3 protein primarily in astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing C3 colocalization with GFAP (astrocyte marker) in Figure 1G.

claim: REV-ERBα deletion increased microglial phagocytosis of synapses in the CA3 region of the hippocampus.
source: REV-ERBα deletion increased microglial phagocytosis of synapses and synapse loss in the CA3 region of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2F showing increased Iba1-CD68-Synaptophysin colocalization and electron microscopy data in Figure 2I.

claim: REV-ERBα deletion causes synapse loss in the CA3 region of the hippocampus.
source: REV-ERBα deletion increased microglial phagocytosis of synapses and synapse loss in the CA3 region of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by synaptic volume quantification data in Figure 3A-G showing decreased synaptophysin, homer1, and synaptoporin staining.

claim: There is diurnal variation in the degree of microglial synaptic phagocytosis which is antiphase to REV-ERBα expression.
source: Finally, we observed diurnal variation in the degree of microglial synaptic phagocytosis which was antiphase to REV-ERBα expression.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C showing increased synaptic engulfment at ZT17 (11PM) compared to ZT5 (11AM) in WT mice.

claim: Global REV-ERBα deletion abrogates daily variation in microglial synaptic phagocytosis.
source: This daily variation in microglial synaptic phagocytosis was abrogated by global REV-ERBα deletion, which caused persistently elevated synaptic phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C showing no time-of-day difference in synaptic engulfment in RKO mice.

claim: Global REV-ERBα deletion causes persistently elevated synaptic phagocytosis.
source: This daily variation in microglial synaptic phagocytosis was abrogated by global REV-ERBα deletion, which caused persistently elevated synaptic phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C showing elevated synaptic engulfment at both timepoints in RKO mice.

claim: The BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis regulates complement expression in the brain.
source: This work uncovers the BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis as a regulator of complement expression and synaptic phagocytosis in the brain, linking circadian proteins to synaptic regulation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experiments showing complement gene upregulation in BMAL1 and REV-ERBα knockout mice.

claim: The BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis regulates synaptic phagocytosis in the brain.
source: This work uncovers the BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis as a regulator of complement expression and synaptic phagocytosis in the brain, linking circadian proteins to synaptic regulation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased microglial synaptic phagocytosis in REV-ERBα knockout mice.

claim: BMAL1 is a bHLH-PAS transcription factor at the core of the circadian clock's positive limb.
source: At the core of the clock's positive limb is the bHLH-PAS transcription factor BMAL1, which heterodimerizes with CLOCK or NPAS2 to drive the transcription of large sets of clock-controlled genes (Mohawk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms, supported by citation to Mohawk et al., 2012.

claim: BMAL1 heterodimerizes with CLOCK or NPAS2 to drive transcription of clock-controlled genes.
source: At the core of the clock's positive limb is the bHLH-PAS transcription factor BMAL1, which heterodimerizes with CLOCK or NPAS2 to drive the transcription of large sets of clock-controlled genes (Mohawk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms, supported by citation to Mohawk et al., 2012.

claim: BMAL1 transcriptional targets include CRY and PER proteins.
source: BMAL1 transcriptional targets include the negative limb feedback regulator CRY and PER proteins, as well as REV-ERBα and β, nuclear receptors which can also inhibit the actions of the positive limb (Preitner et al., 2002; Retnakaran et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms, supported by citations to Preitner et al., 2002 and Retnakaran et al., 1994.

claim: BMAL1 transcriptional targets include REV-ERBα and β.
source: BMAL1 transcriptional targets include the negative limb feedback regulator CRY and PER proteins, as well as REV-ERBα and β, nuclear receptors which can also inhibit the actions of the positive limb (Preitner et al., 2002; Retnakaran et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms, supported by citations to Preitner et al., 2002 and Retnakaran et al., 1994.

claim: REV-ERBα and β are nuclear receptors that can inhibit the actions of the circadian clock's positive limb.
source: BMAL1 transcriptional targets include the negative limb feedback regulator CRY and PER proteins, as well as REV-ERBα and β, nuclear receptors which can also inhibit the actions of the positive limb (Preitner et al., 2002; Retnakaran et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms, supported by citations to Preitner et al., 2002 and Retnakaran et al., 1994.

claim: Disruption of circadian machinery is associated with cancer, diabetes, and neurodegeneration.
source: Disruption of this circadian machinery is associated with various pathophysiological states including cancer, diabetes, and neurodegeneration (Everett and Lazar, 2014; Musiek and Holtzman, 2016; Sulli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review articles (Everett and Lazar, 2014; Musiek and Holtzman, 2016; Sulli et al., 2018).

claim: Deletion of BMAL1 abrogates circadian clock function.
source: Deletion of BMAL1 abrogates circadian clock function and leads to an ~80% decrease in REV-ERBα expression in the brain (Musiek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Musiek et al., 2013.

claim: Deletion of BMAL1 leads to an ~80% decrease in REV-ERBα expression in the brain.
source: Deletion of BMAL1 abrogates circadian clock function and leads to an ~80% decrease in REV-ERBα expression in the brain (Musiek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Musiek et al., 2013.

claim: REV-ERBα functions as a transcriptional repressor in many tissues.
source: REV-ERBα functions as a transcriptional repressor in many tissues and has been implicated in regulation of metabolism and inflammation (Everett and Lazar, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Everett and Lazar, 2014.

claim: REV-ERBα has been implicated in regulation of metabolism and inflammation.
source: REV-ERBα functions as a transcriptional repressor in many tissues and has been implicated in regulation of metabolism and inflammation (Everett and Lazar, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Everett and Lazar, 2014.

claim: Deletion of BMAL1 causes neuroinflammation.
source: Previous work from our group shows that deletion of BMAL1 or its downstream target REV-ERBα causes neuroinflammation and impaired brain functional connectivity (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα causes neuroinflammation.
source: Previous work from our group shows that deletion of BMAL1 or its downstream target REV-ERBα causes neuroinflammation and impaired brain functional connectivity (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).

claim: Deletion of BMAL1 causes impaired brain functional connectivity.
source: Previous work from our group shows that deletion of BMAL1 or its downstream target REV-ERBα causes neuroinflammation and impaired brain functional connectivity (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα causes impaired brain functional connectivity.
source: Previous work from our group shows that deletion of BMAL1 or its downstream target REV-ERBα causes neuroinflammation and impaired brain functional connectivity (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).

claim: Diminished BMAL1 expression has been described in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Diminished BMAL1 and REV-ERBα expression have also been described in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease (AD)(Lee et al., 2020; Stevanovic et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2020 and Stevanovic et al., 2017.

claim: Diminished REV-ERBα expression has been described in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Diminished BMAL1 and REV-ERBα expression have also been described in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease (AD)(Lee et al., 2020; Stevanovic et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2020 and Stevanovic et al., 2017.

claim: Memory-associated, synapse-rich regions such as the hippocampus are affected early in Alzheimer's disease.
source: In AD, memory-associated, synapse-rich regions such as the hippocampus are affected early in the disease course (Braak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology, supported by citation to Braak et al., 2006.

claim: Synaptic loss precedes neuronal death in neurodegeneration.
source: Synaptic loss also precedes neuronal death in neurodegeneration (Selkoe, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neurodegenerative disease, supported by citation to Selkoe, 2002.

claim: Circadian dysfunction is a well-described symptom of Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Circadian dysfunction is also a well-described symptom of AD and other neurodegenerative diseases (Musiek and Holtzman, 2016; Videnovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Musiek and Holtzman, 2016 and Videnovic et al., 2014.

claim: Synapses labeled with C1q and C3 are pruned by microglia during development.
source: Synapses labeled with the opsonins C1q and C3 (Stevens et al., 2007) were first described to be pruned by microglia during development (Schafer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Stevens et al., 2007 and Schafer et al., 2012.

claim: C4 protein contributes to synaptic pruning by microglia in vivo.
source: C4 protein, encoded by the mouse C4b gene, also contributes to synaptic pruning by microglia in vivo (Sekar et al., 2016; Comer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sekar et al., 2016 and Comer et al., 2020.

claim: C4 protein is encoded by the mouse C4b gene.
source: C4 protein, encoded by the mouse C4b gene, also contributes to synaptic pruning by microglia in vivo (Sekar et al., 2016; Comer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mouse genetics.

claim: Complement-dependent microglial synaptic pruning has been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: Complement-dependent microglial synaptic pruning has also been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases (Hong et al., 2016; Litvinchuk et al., 2018; Sekar et al., 2016; Werneburg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Hong et al., 2016; Litvinchuk et al., 2018; Sekar et al., 2016; Werneburg et al., 2020).

claim: Microglial activation is subject to circadian regulation.
source: Microglial activation is subject to circadian regulation (Fonken et al., 2015; Hayashi et al., 2013), and we have previously described that deletion of BMAL1 or REV-ERBα can induce microglial activation (Griffin et al., 2019; Musiek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fonken et al., 2015 and Hayashi et al., 2013.

claim: C1qc, C1qb, C1qa, and C1ra transcripts were increased in BMKO hippocampus.
source: Other complement-related transcripts including C1qc, C1qb, C1qa, and C1ra were also increased in BMKO hippocampus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: C4b was upregulated in cerebral cortex samples from brain-specific Bmal1 KO mice (Nestin-Cre;Bmal1f/f).
source: Analysis of second published microarray dataset from our group which was derived from cerebral cortex samples from brain-specific Bmal1 KO mice (Nestin-Cre;Bmal1f/f) mice (Lananna et al., 2018) also revealed specific upregulation of C4b, but less so for other complement factors (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A and cited from Lananna et al., 2018.

claim: C4b was increased in cerebral cortex samples from 4mo tamoxifen-inducible global BMAL1 KO mice in which Bmal1 was deleted at 2mo.
source: C4b was similarly increased in cerebral cortex samples from 4mo tamoxifen-inducible global BMAL1 KO mice (CAG-CreERT2;Bmal1f/f) in which Bmal1 was deleted at 2mo, demonstrating that this is not a developmental phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The upregulation of C4b following BMAL1 deletion is not a developmental phenomenon.
source: C4b was similarly increased in cerebral cortex samples from 4mo tamoxifen-inducible global BMAL1 KO mice (CAG-CreERT2;Bmal1f/f) in which Bmal1 was deleted at 2mo, demonstrating that this is not a developmental phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that inducible deletion at 2 months of age still causes C4b upregulation, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: C4b mRNA was strongly induced in neuron-specific Bmal1 KO mice.
source: Notably, C4b mRNA was strongly induced in the neuron-specific Bmal1 KO mice, while C3 was not (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: C3 mRNA was not induced in neuron-specific Bmal1 KO mice.
source: Notably, C4b mRNA was strongly induced in the neuron-specific Bmal1 KO mice, while C3 was not (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: C4b was induced to a lesser degree in astrocyte-specific Bmal1 KO mice.
source: C4b was also induced to a lesser degree in astrocyte-specific Bmal1 KO mice, although C3 was not (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: C3 was not induced in astrocyte-specific Bmal1 KO mice.
source: C4b was also induced to a lesser degree in astrocyte-specific Bmal1 KO mice, although C3 was not (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Neither C4b nor C3 was induced in microglia-specific Bmal1 KO mice under basal conditions.
source: Under basal conditions, neither C4b nor C3 was induced in microglia specific Bmal1 KO mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Deletion of Bmal1 in primary neurons via AAV8-Cre suppressed Nr1d1 (REV-ERBα) by 85%.
source: Deletion of Bmal1 in primary Bmal1fl/fl neuron cultures via infection with an AAV8-Cre viral vector (versus AAV8-eGFP control) suppressed the BMAL1 transcriptional target Nr1d1 (which encodes REV-ERBα) by 85% and induced C4b expression but caused no increase in C3 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary neuron cultures shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Deletion of Bmal1 in primary neurons induced C4b expression.
source: Deletion of Bmal1 in primary Bmal1fl/fl neuron cultures via infection with an AAV8-Cre viral vector (versus AAV8-eGFP control) suppressed the BMAL1 transcriptional target Nr1d1 (which encodes REV-ERBα) by 85% and induced C4b expression but caused no increase in C3 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary neuron cultures shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Deletion of Bmal1 in primary neurons caused no increase in C3.
source: Deletion of Bmal1 in primary Bmal1fl/fl neuron cultures via infection with an AAV8-Cre viral vector (versus AAV8-eGFP control) suppressed the BMAL1 transcriptional target Nr1d1 (which encodes REV-ERBα) by 85% and induced C4b expression but caused no increase in C3 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary neuron cultures shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Bmal1 deletion in primary neurons increased expression of Fabp7.
source: Bmal1 deletion also increased expression of Fabp7 (Figure 1E), a known target of REV-ERBα-mediated transcriptional repression (Schnell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Schnell et al., 2014.

claim: Fabp7 is a known target of REV-ERBα-mediated transcriptional repression.
source: Bmal1 deletion also increased expression of Fabp7 (Figure 1E), a known target of REV-ERBα-mediated transcriptional repression (Schnell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Schnell et al., 2014.

claim: REV-ERBα mRNA (Nr1d1) is suppressed by ~80% in the brain following brain-specific Bmal1 deletion.
source: As REV-ERBα mRNA (Nr1d1) is also suppressed by ~80% in the brain following brain-specific Bmal1 deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), our data suggested that the upregulation of C4b gene expression observed with loss of BMAL1 could be mediated by transcriptional de-repression as consequence of downstream REV-ERBα loss.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The upregulation of C4b gene expression observed with loss of BMAL1 could be mediated by transcriptional de-repression as a consequence of downstream REV-ERBα loss.
source: As REV-ERBα mRNA (Nr1d1) is also suppressed by ~80% in the brain following brain-specific Bmal1 deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), our data suggested that the upregulation of C4b gene expression observed with loss of BMAL1 could be mediated by transcriptional de-repression as consequence of downstream REV-ERBα loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BMAL1 deletion suppresses REV-ERBα and increases C4b, and REV-ERBα is a transcriptional repressor.

claim: Global deletion of REV-ERBα caused striking increases in C4b, C3, and other complement transcripts in the hippocampus.
source: Accordingly, global deletion of REV-ERBα caused striking increases in C4b, C3, and other complement transcripts in the hippocampus as assessed by microarray analysis (Figure 1A) and confirmed in separate samples by qPCR (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Figure 1A and qPCR data in Figure 1F.

claim: Increased C3 protein expression was observed in activated astrocytes in the hippocampus of 5mo REV-ERBα KO mice.
source: Increased C3 protein expression was observed in activated astrocytes (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) in the hippocampus of 5mo REV-ERBα KO (RKO) mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing C3-GFAP colocalization in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was less overlap of C3 expression and the microglial marker Iba1 in RKO mice.
source: There was less overlap of C3 expression and the microglial marker Iba1 (Figure 1H), although microglial C3 expression did increase in RKO brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1H and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Microglial C3 expression increased in RKO brain.
source: There was less overlap of C3 expression and the microglial marker Iba1 (Figure 1H), although microglial C3 expression did increase in RKO brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: REV-ERBα directly represses C4b expression in neurons and astrocytes.
source: The finding that Bmal1 deletion in neurons (and to a less degree astrocytes) induces C4b mRNA but that C3 only increases in global BMKO and RKO mice suggests that REV-ERBα directly represses C4b expression in neurons and astrocytes, but the induction of C3 in both BMKO and RKO brain is likely secondary to a multicellular inflammatory glial activation which occurs over time.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of C4b induction in cell-type-specific knockouts versus global knockouts.

claim: The induction of C3 in BMKO and RKO brain is likely secondary to a multicellular inflammatory glial activation which occurs over time.
source: The finding that Bmal1 deletion in neurons (and to a less degree astrocytes) induces C4b mRNA but that C3 only increases in global BMKO and RKO mice suggests that REV-ERBα directly represses C4b expression in neurons and astrocytes, but the induction of C3 in both BMKO and RKO brain is likely secondary to a multicellular inflammatory glial activation which occurs over time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C3 only increases in global knockouts but not cell-type-specific knockouts.

claim: Global REV-ERBα deletion induced microglial activation in vivo.
source: We previously demonstrated that global REV-ERBα deletion induced microglial activation in vivo (Griffin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019).

claim: There was a 13.6-fold increase in engulfed synaptic material in the hippocampus of RKO mice compared to WT littermates.
source: In all, we noted a 13.6-fold increase in engulfed synaptic material in the hippocampus of RKO mice compared to their WT littermates (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: RKO microglia had synaptic material in both the microglial process and cell body.
source: In the RKO microglia, we observed synaptic material in the microglial process and cell body (Figure 2Eii, Eiii), whereas WT microglia only had engulfed synaptic material in the cell body (Figure 2Ei).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2E.

claim: WT microglia only had engulfed synaptic material in the cell body.
source: In the RKO microglia, we observed synaptic material in the microglial process and cell body (Figure 2Eii, Eiii), whereas WT microglia only had engulfed synaptic material in the cell body (Figure 2Ei).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Scanning electron microscopy confirmed an increased number of presynaptic terminals within or in contact with microglia in the hippocampus of RKO mice compared to WT.
source: Using this method, we visually confirmed an increased number of presynaptic terminals within or in contact with microglia in the hippocampus of RKO mice compared to WT (Figure 2G and H, 2H(i-v), 2I).
evidence: This is supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Sirpa gene expression was downregulated in RKO mice.
source: We also noted downregulation in the expression of the Sirpa gene in our RKO mice which codes for the protein SIRPα (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SIRPα was recently described as a surface receptor on microglia that serves as a receptor for a 'do-not-eat-me' signal.
source: SIRPα was recently described as a surface receptor on microglia that serves as a receptor for a 'do-not-eat-me' signal (Lehrman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lehrman et al., 2018.

claim: Sirpa was not downregulated in Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice.
source: Notably, Sirpa was not downregulated in Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice (Figure 1A), which have normal microglial BMAL1 and REV-ERBα expression, suggesting a possible cell-autonomous effect of REV-ERBα on microglial Sirpa expression.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice have normal microglial BMAL1 and REV-ERBα expression.
source: Notably, Sirpa was not downregulated in Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice (Figure 1A), which have normal microglial BMAL1 and REV-ERBα expression, suggesting a possible cell-autonomous effect of REV-ERBα on microglial Sirpa expression.
evidence: This is based on knowledge that Nestin-Cre does not delete genes in microglia.

claim: There is a possible cell-autonomous effect of REV-ERBα on microglial Sirpa expression.
source: Notably, Sirpa was not downregulated in Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice (Figure 1A), which have normal microglial BMAL1 and REV-ERBα expression, suggesting a possible cell-autonomous effect of REV-ERBα on microglial Sirpa expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sirpa is only downregulated when microglia lack REV-ERBα.

claim: REV-ERBα deletion induces synaptic engulfment.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that REV-ERBα deletion induces synaptic engulfment.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple lines of evidence showing increased synaptic phagocytosis in RKO mice.

claim: There was a significant decrease in synaptic volume in the CA3 region of the hippocampus in RKO mice by synaptophysin staining.
source: In RKO mice, we observed a significant decrease in the synaptic volume in the CA3 region of the hippocampus by synaptophysin staining (Figure 3A), homer1 staining (Figure 3B), and their colocalization (Figure 3C) compared to their WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant decrease in synaptic volume in the CA3 region of the hippocampus in RKO mice by homer1 staining.
source: In RKO mice, we observed a significant decrease in the synaptic volume in the CA3 region of the hippocampus by synaptophysin staining (Figure 3A), homer1 staining (Figure 3B), and their colocalization (Figure 3C) compared to their WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a significant decrease in synaptic volume in the CA3 region of the hippocampus in RKO mice by synaptophysin-homer1 colocalization.
source: In RKO mice, we observed a significant decrease in the synaptic volume in the CA3 region of the hippocampus by synaptophysin staining (Figure 3A), homer1 staining (Figure 3B), and their colocalization (Figure 3C) compared to their WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a decrease in the number of synapses in the RKO mouse CA3 by scanning electron microscopy.
source: To further confirm these results, we counted synapses in large area SEM images from the stratum lucidum of WT or RKO mice. Again, we noted a decrease in the number of synapses in the RKO mouse CA3 by SEM, as compared to their WT littermates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a decrease in synaptic volume in CA3 of RKO mice using synaptoporin staining.
source: Again, we observed a similar decrease in synaptic volume in CA3 of RKO mice compared to their WT littermates using synaptoporin staining (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 3E and 3G.

claim: Synaptoporin is enriched in the mossy fiber synapses of the hippocampus.
source: Synaptoporin was used because it is enriched in the mossy fiber synapses of the hippocampus (Singec et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Singec et al., 2002.

claim: There were no significant differences in synaptic volumes between WT and RKO mice in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe significant differences in synaptic volumes between WT and RKO mice in the CA1 region of the hippocampus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that some terminals may be more susceptible to loss than others.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some synaptic terminals may be more susceptible to loss than others.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe significant differences in synaptic volumes between WT and RKO mice in the CA1 region of the hippocampus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that some terminals may be more susceptible to loss than others.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CA3 synapses are lost but CA1 synapses are not in RKO mice.

claim: There was no significant difference in neuronal nuclear width of the dentate gyrus between WT and RKO mice.
source: To determine whether the loss in synapses was due to a loss of neuronal cell bodies, we quantified the volume and width of neuronal nuclei of the dentate gyrus, which project to CA3, via NeuN staining. We found no significant difference between the neuronal nuclear width or volumes of the dentate gyrus between the WT and RKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by NeuN staining quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant difference in neuronal nuclear volume of the dentate gyrus between WT and RKO mice.
source: To determine whether the loss in synapses was due to a loss of neuronal cell bodies, we quantified the volume and width of neuronal nuclei of the dentate gyrus, which project to CA3, via NeuN staining. We found no significant difference between the neuronal nuclear width or volumes of the dentate gyrus between the WT and RKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by NeuN staining quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dentate gyrus projects to CA3.
source: To determine whether the loss in synapses was due to a loss of neuronal cell bodies, we quantified the volume and width of neuronal nuclei of the dentate gyrus, which project to CA3, via NeuN staining.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hippocampal anatomy.

claim: There was no change in 3-nitrotyrosine staining in the dentate gyrus of RKO mice.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any change in 3-nitrotyrosine staining in the dentate gyrus, suggesting there is no increase in neuronal nitrosative stress in RKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by 3-nitrotyrosine staining quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is no increase in neuronal nitrosative stress in RKO mice.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any change in 3-nitrotyrosine staining in the dentate gyrus, suggesting there is no increase in neuronal nitrosative stress in RKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in 3-nitrotyrosine staining, which is a marker of nitrosative stress.

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα results in robust synaptic loss in the CA3 region without obvious neuronal loss.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that deletion of REV-ERBα results in robust synaptic loss in the CA3 region without obvious neuronal loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of decreased synapses but no change in neuronal cell body markers.

claim: In mouse cerebral cortex and ventral midbrain, REV-ERBα displays daily oscillation in mRNA level with its peak around zeitgeber time (ZT) eight and its trough around ZT20.
source: In mouse cerebral cortex and ventral midbrain, REV-ERBα displays daily oscillation in mRNA level with its peak around zeitgeber time (ZT) eight and its trough around ZT20 (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: Microglial activation oscillates with low activation at ZT5 and high activation at ZT17.
source: We have also previously described oscillations in microglial activation, with low activation at ZT5 and high activation at ZT17 (Griffin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019).

claim: Microglia from the CA3 region of the hippocampus in WT mice sacrificed at ZT17 showed significantly more engulfed presynaptic protein than those at ZT5.
source: Microglia from the CA3 region of the hippocampus in WT mice sacrificed at ZT17 showed significantly more engulfed presynaptic protein than those at ZT5 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RKO mice harvested at ZT5 and 17 showed a persistently increased level of synaptic engulfment in microglia with no time-of-day variation.
source: When compared to the WT mice, RKO mice harvested at ZT5 and 17 showed a persistently increased level of synaptic engulfment in microglia, but with no time-of-day variation (Figure 4C), suggesting that daily oscillations in REV-ERBα may mediate rhythms in microglial synaptic phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Daily oscillations in REV-ERBα may mediate rhythms in microglial synaptic phagocytosis.
source: When compared to the WT mice, RKO mice harvested at ZT5 and 17 showed a persistently increased level of synaptic engulfment in microglia, but with no time-of-day variation (Figure 4C), suggesting that daily oscillations in REV-ERBα may mediate rhythms in microglial synaptic phagocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis is lost when REV-ERBα is deleted.

claim: There was a higher number of presynaptic terminals in contact with and within microglia at ZT17 compared to ZT5.
source: To further establish these findings, we used large area SEM to count the number of presynaptic terminals in contact with or within microglia at ZT17, and compared to mice harvested at ZT5 (shown in Figure 2G–H). In that experiment, we also noted a higher number of presynaptic terminals in contact with and within the microglia at ZT17 (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Microglia at 11PM (ZT17) showed a qualitative increase in mCherry engulfment compared to those at 11AM (ZT5) in Cx3cr1GFP mice injected with AAV-Camk2a-mCherry.
source: As a final confirmation of this finding, we injected Cx3cr1GFP mice, which express GFP in microglia (Jung et al., 2000), with an AAV-Camk2a-mCherry viral vector in the retrospenial cortex, to express mCherry in neurons. 4 weeks later, we collected brain samples at ZT5 and 17, and calculated the volume of mCherry+ material in individual GFP+ microglia. We observed that microglia at 11PM (ZT17) showed a qualitative increase in mCherry engulfment as compared to those at 11AM (ZT5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a REV-ERBα-dependent rhythm for the engulfment of neuronal materials by microglia in the brain.
source: Overall, our data establish a REV-ERBα-dependent rhythm for the engulfment of neuronal materials by microglia in the brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple experiments showing time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis that is lost in RKO mice.

claim: Loss of BMAL1 causes upregulation of complement gene C4b in neurons and astrocytes.
source: The current study shows that loss of the circadian protein BMAL1 causes upregulation of complement gene C4b in neurons and astrocytes, as well as increase astrocytic C3 expression, changes which are recapitulated by loss of downstream REV-ERBα-mediated transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is supported by data from tissue-specific knockout mice shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Loss of BMAL1 causes increased astrocytic C3 expression.
source: The current study shows that loss of the circadian protein BMAL1 causes upregulation of complement gene C4b in neurons and astrocytes, as well as increase astrocytic C3 expression, changes which are recapitulated by loss of downstream REV-ERBα-mediated transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing C3-GFAP colocalization in Figure 1G.

claim: Changes in complement expression caused by BMAL1 loss are recapitulated by loss of downstream REV-ERBα-mediated transcriptional repression.
source: The current study shows that loss of the circadian protein BMAL1 causes upregulation of complement gene C4b in neurons and astrocytes, as well as increase astrocytic C3 expression, changes which are recapitulated by loss of downstream REV-ERBα-mediated transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is supported by data showing similar complement gene upregulation in both BMAL1 and REV-ERBα knockout mice.

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα leads to microglial activation.
source: Deletion of REV-ERBα leads to microglial activation, increased C4b and C3 mRNA expression, increased astrocyte C3 protein expression, and increased microglial synaptic phagocytosis in CA3 region of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Griffin et al., 2019) and data in the current study.

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα leads to increased C4b and C3 mRNA expression.
source: Deletion of REV-ERBα leads to microglial activation, increased C4b and C3 mRNA expression, increased astrocyte C3 protein expression, and increased microglial synaptic phagocytosis in CA3 region of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Deletion of REV-ERBα leads to increased astrocyte C3 protein expression.
source: Deletion of REV-ERBα leads to microglial activation, increased C4b and C3 mRNA expression, increased astrocyte C3 protein expression, and increased microglial synaptic phagocytosis in CA3 region of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There is a time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis in the hippocampus of WT mice which is antiphase to REV-ERBα levels.
source: Finally, we demonstrate a time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis in the hippocampus of WT mice which is antiphase to REV-ERBα levels and lost after REV-ERBα deletion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C showing increased phagocytosis at ZT17 when REV-ERBα is low.

claim: Time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis is lost after REV-ERBα deletion.
source: Finally, we demonstrate a time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis in the hippocampus of WT mice which is antiphase to REV-ERBα levels and lost after REV-ERBα deletion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C showing no time-of-day variation in RKO mice.

claim: The BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis regulates daily rhythms in synaptic phagocytosis.
source: Our findings suggest that the BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis regulates daily rhythms in synaptic phagocytosis, and that loss of REV-ERBα de-represses complement gene expression and locks the brain in a pro-phagocytic state.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis is lost when REV-ERBα is deleted.

claim: Loss of REV-ERBα de-represses complement gene expression and locks the brain in a pro-phagocytic state.
source: Our findings suggest that the BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis regulates daily rhythms in synaptic phagocytosis, and that loss of REV-ERBα de-represses complement gene expression and locks the brain in a pro-phagocytic state.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RKO mice have persistently elevated complement expression and synaptic phagocytosis at all times.

claim: The mechanisms by which BMAL1 deletion leads to increased C4b expression likely depend on REV-ERBα.
source: The mechanisms by which BMAL1 deletion leads to increased C4b expression are complex and multicellular but likely depend on REV-ERBα, although contributions of other pathways cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that REV-ERBα deletion phenocopies the complement gene expression increases seen in Bmal1 KO brain.

claim: REV-ERBα expression is decreased by ~85% following BMAL1 deletion.
source: REV-ERBα expression is decreased by ~85% following BMAL1 deletion, and REV-ERBα deletion phenocopies the complement gene expression increases seen in Bmal1 KO brain.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: REV-ERBα deletion phenocopies the complement gene expression increases seen in Bmal1 KO brain.
source: REV-ERBα expression is decreased by ~85% following BMAL1 deletion, and REV-ERBα deletion phenocopies the complement gene expression increases seen in Bmal1 KO brain.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of microarray data from BMAL1 KO and REV-ERBα KO mice shown in Figure 1A.

claim: REV-ERBα functions as a transcriptional repressor.
source: Indeed, it is well established that REV-ERBα functions as a transcriptional repressor (Harding and Lazar, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Harding and Lazar, 1995.

claim: Loss of REV-ERBα-mediated repression is a general mechanism governing increased transcript expression following BMAL1 deletion.
source: Loss of REV-ERBα-mediated repression is a general mechanism governing increased transcript expression following BMAL1 deletion - as evidenced by strong upregulation of the REV-ERBα repression target Fabp7 following BMAL1 deletion (Schnell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fabp7, a known REV-ERBα target, is upregulated following BMAL1 deletion.

claim: No REV-ERBα ChIP-seq peaks corresponding to C4b were found in an existing database from brain tissue.
source: Notably, we queried an existing REV-ERBα ChIP-seq database from brain tissue (Zhang et al., 2015), and did not find any peaks corresponding to C4b.
evidence: This is based on analysis of an existing ChIP-seq database cited (Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: REV-ERBα is known to regulate transcription by regulating enhancer function and eRNA expression to alter gene expression in trans.
source: However, REV-ERBα is known to regulate transcription not only by direct binding to RORE and RevDR2 sites but also by regulating enhancer function and eRNA expression to alter gene expression in trans (Lam et al., 2013), and by altering chromatin looping (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lam et al., 2013.

claim: REV-ERBα is known to regulate transcription by altering chromatin looping.
source: However, REV-ERBα is known to regulate transcription not only by direct binding to RORE and RevDR2 sites but also by regulating enhancer function and eRNA expression to alter gene expression in trans (Lam et al., 2013), and by altering chromatin looping (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kim et al., 2018.

claim: REV-ERBα likely regulates C4b expression in alternative ways not apparent by typical ChIP-seq.
source: Thus, it is likely that REV-ERBα regulates C4b expression in one of these alternative ways which is not apparent by typical ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of direct ChIP-seq peaks but clear functional evidence of regulation.

claim: The BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis controls C4b expression in neurons and astrocytes, but not in microglia.
source: Tissue-specific deletion of BMAL1 shows that this BMAL1-REV-ERBα axis controls C4b expression in neurons and astrocytes, but not in microglia.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from tissue-specific knockout mice shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Recent single-nucleus RNAseq data suggests that C4b is prominently expressed in oligodendrocytes.
source: Recent single-nucleus RNAseq data suggests that C4b is prominently expressed in oligodendrocytes (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: C4b expression is presumably low in neurons and astrocytes under normal conditions but is increased by BMAL1 or REV-ERBα deletion.
source: Presumably, C4b expression is low in neurons and astrocytes under normal conditions but is increased by BMAL1 or REV-ERBα deletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C4b is upregulated in knockout mice.

claim: Deletion of C4b prevents accumulation of C3 protein at synapses, as C4 protein is upstream of C3 activation in the classical complement pathway.
source: Work from the Stevens and McCarroll labs identified C4b expression in neurons which then tagged synapses and facilitated synaptic pruning, and showed that deletion of C4b prevents accumulation of C3 protein at synapses, as C4 protein in upstream of C3 activation in the classical complement pathway (Sekar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Sekar et al., 2016.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of mouse C4 can drive microglial synaptic phagocytosis and cause functional connectivity deficits in mice.
source: Moreover, neuronal overexpression of mouse C4 can drive microglial synaptic phagocytosis and cause functional connectivity deficits in mice (Comer et al., 2020), two phenotypes observed by us in RKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Comer et al., 2020.

claim: Bmal1 KO and RKO mice at 5–6mo show an increase in C3 transcript and C3 protein in astrocytes.
source: Bmal1 KO and RKO mice at 5–6mo also show an increase in C3 transcript and C3 protein in astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Tissue-specific Bmal1 deletion in neurons or astrocytes causes pronounced C4b increases but no C3 increases.
source: However, tissue-specific Bmal1 deletion in neurons or astrocytes causes pronounced C4b increases but no C3 increases, suggesting that C3 expression in astrocytes and microglia is a secondary response to increased neuroinflammation in aged global Bmal1 KO or RKO mouse brain.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from tissue-specific knockout mice shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: C3 expression in astrocytes and microglia is a secondary response to increased neuroinflammation in aged global Bmal1 KO or RKO mouse brain.
source: However, tissue-specific Bmal1 deletion in neurons or astrocytes causes pronounced C4b increases but no C3 increases, suggesting that C3 expression in astrocytes and microglia is a secondary response to increased neuroinflammation in aged global Bmal1 KO or RKO mouse brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C3 only increases in global knockouts but not cell-type-specific knockouts.

claim: Global inducible Bmal1 KO mice do not show C3 induction at 2mo post-tamoxifen despite high C4b expression.
source: Global inducible Bmal1 KO mice also do not show C3 induction at 2mo post-tamoxifen (despite high C4b expression), as these mice have not developed a full neuroinflammatory response at that age.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Full induction of C3 in BMKO and RKO brain requires a multicellular, time-dependent inflammatory response involving microglia.
source: Our data suggest that full induction of C3 in BMKO and RKO brain requires a multicellular, time-dependent inflammatory response involving microglia, as Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice, which have Bmal1 deletion in neurons and astrocytes but not microglia, have increased C4b expression but normal C3 and Sirpa levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice (which lack microglial deletion) do not show C3 upregulation.

claim: Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice have Bmal1 deletion in neurons and astrocytes but not microglia.
source: Our data suggest that full induction of C3 in BMKO and RKO brain requires a multicellular, time-dependent inflammatory response involving microglia, as Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice, which have Bmal1 deletion in neurons and astrocytes but not microglia, have increased C4b expression but normal C3 and Sirpa levels.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about the specificity of Nestin-Cre.

claim: Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice have increased C4b expression but normal C3 and Sirpa levels.
source: Our data suggest that full induction of C3 in BMKO and RKO brain requires a multicellular, time-dependent inflammatory response involving microglia, as Nestin-Cre-Bmal1 KO mice, which have Bmal1 deletion in neurons and astrocytes but not microglia, have increased C4b expression but normal C3 and Sirpa levels.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: REV-ERBα deletion increases microglial activation, Traf2 expression, and increased NFκB signaling.
source: We have previously shown that REV-ERBα deletion increases microglial activation, Traf2 expression, and increased NFκB signaling (Griffin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019).

claim: REV-ERBα loss in microglia may be necessary, but not sufficient, to induce astrocyte C3 expression.
source: Thus, REV-ERBα loss in microglia may be necessary, but not sufficient, to induce astrocyte C3 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C3 is only induced in global knockouts where microglia also lack REV-ERBα.

claim: Activated microglia can readily induce astrocyte C3 in response to LPS.
source: Indeed, activated microglia can readily induce astrocyte C3 in response to LPS (Liddelow et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Liddelow et al., 2017.

claim: NFκB signaling has been shown to increase C3 expression and release from astrocytes.
source: NFκB signaling has also been shown to increase C3 expression and release from astrocytes (Lian et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lian et al., 2015.

claim: C4 loss is associated with less synaptic tagging with C3 and thus less synaptic pruning.
source: Functionally, C4 loss is associated with less synaptic tagging with C3 and thus less synaptic pruning (Sekar et al., 2016), suggesting that C4 expression can drive C3-dependent synapse pruning.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Sekar et al., 2016.

claim: C4 expression can drive C3-dependent synapse pruning.
source: Functionally, C4 loss is associated with less synaptic tagging with C3 and thus less synaptic pruning (Sekar et al., 2016), suggesting that C4 expression can drive C3-dependent synapse pruning.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C4 loss reduces C3 tagging and pruning.

claim: Loss of inhibitory signaling from SIRPα makes microglia more likely to prune synapses.
source: Additionally, we noted that REV-ERBα regulated the microglial 'do-not-eat-me' signal Sirpa (encoding SIRPα) in our microarray data. Loss of inhibitory signaling from SIRPα makes microglia more likely to prune synapses, since SIRPα is primarily expressed on microglia in the CNS (Lehrman et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lehrman et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: SIRPα is primarily expressed on microglia in the CNS.
source: Additionally, we noted that REV-ERBα regulated the microglial 'do-not-eat-me' signal Sirpa (encoding SIRPα) in our microarray data. Loss of inhibitory signaling from SIRPα makes microglia more likely to prune synapses, since SIRPα is primarily expressed on microglia in the CNS (Lehrman et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lehrman et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: De-repression of C4b in neurons and Traf2 in astrocytes and microglia, as well as diminished Sirpa expression in microglia, lead to a 'perfect storm' of complement expression and microglial activation that promotes synaptic phagocytosis.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that de-repression of C4b in neurons and Traf2 in astrocytes and microglia, as well as diminished Sirpa expression in microglia, lead to a 'perfect storm' of complement expression and microglial activation that promotes synaptic phagocytosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple observations of complement upregulation, microglial activation, and increased synaptic phagocytosis.

claim: CA2/3 mossy fiber synaptic boutons are large and easily labeled with synaptic vesicle markers.
source: We focused on the CA2/3 mossy fiber synaptic boutons because they are large and easily labeled with synaptic vesicle markers – in this case synaptoporin and synaptophysin (Grosse et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hippocampal anatomy, supported by citation to Grosse et al., 1998.

claim: There may be regional variability in BMAL1-REV-ERBα mediated synaptic pruning.
source: However, we did not observe synapse loss in the CA1 region, which may represent a regional variability in BMAL1-REV-ERBα mediated synaptic pruning.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CA3 synapses are lost but CA1 synapses are not.

claim: Certain synapses may be more susceptible to pruning than others.
source: Certainly, it is possible that certain synapses are more susceptible to pruning than others, and this should be addressed in the future.
evidence: This is speculation based on the regional differences observed.

claim: REV-ERBα deletion does not cause overt neurodegenerative response in the dentate gyrus.
source: However, the absence of neuronal cell body loss or increased 3-nitrotyrosine in the dentate gyrus of RKO mice shows that there is no overt neurodegenerative response.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in NeuN and 3-nitrotyrosine staining.

claim: Dentate gyrus granule cells give rise to the mossy fiber boutons in the CA3.
source: These dentate gyrus granule cells give rise to the mossy fiber boutons in the CA3 (Scharfman and Myers, 2012), which are clearly decreased in RKO mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hippocampal anatomy, supported by citation to Scharfman and Myers, 2012.

claim: The effect of REV-ERBα appears to be specific to the synapses.
source: Thus, the effect of REV-ERBα appears to be specific to the synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of synapse loss without neuronal cell body loss.

claim: Time-of-day changes in microglial morphology were abrogated by REV-ERBα deletion.
source: However, we have previously reported that time-of-day changes in microglial morphology were abrogated by REV-ERBα deletion (Griffin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' group (Griffin et al., 2019).

claim: REV-ERBα mediates daily changes in the degree of microglial synaptic engulfment.
source: This data parallels our previous findings with microglial morphologic changes and suggests that REV-ERBα mediates daily changes in the degree of microglial synaptic engulfment, with both microglial activation and synaptic phagocytosis increasing when REV-ERBα levels are low.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that time-of-day variation in synaptic phagocytosis is lost in RKO mice.

claim: Both microglial activation and synaptic phagocytosis increase when REV-ERBα levels are low.
source: This data parallels our previous findings with microglial morphologic changes and suggests that REV-ERBα mediates daily changes in the degree of microglial synaptic engulfment, with both microglial activation and synaptic phagocytosis increasing when REV-ERBα levels are low.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased phagocytosis at ZT17 when REV-ERBα is low.

claim: REV-ERBα deletion appears to lock the system in one of the extremes of naturally occurring diurnal variation.
source: Accordingly, REV-ERBα deletion appears to lock the system in one of the extremes of this naturally occurring diurnal variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RKO mice have persistently elevated phagocytosis at all times.

claim: RKO mice have subtle alterations in sleep but show grossly normal circadian rhythms in activity.
source: RKO have subtle alterations in sleep but show grossly normal circadian rhythms in activity and are not sleep deprived (Mang et al., 2016), suggesting that sleep alteration is a possible but less likely contributor to the synaptic phenotypes in RKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mang et al., 2016.

claim: RKO mice are not sleep deprived.
source: RKO have subtle alterations in sleep but show grossly normal circadian rhythms in activity and are not sleep deprived (Mang et al., 2016), suggesting that sleep alteration is a possible but less likely contributor to the synaptic phenotypes in RKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mang et al., 2016.

claim: Sleep alteration is a possible but less likely contributor to the synaptic phenotypes in RKO mice.
source: RKO have subtle alterations in sleep but show grossly normal circadian rhythms in activity and are not sleep deprived (Mang et al., 2016), suggesting that sleep alteration is a possible but less likely contributor to the synaptic phenotypes in RKO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RKO mice are not sleep deprived.

claim: A previous study in the rat prefrontal cortex found that synaptic elimination was highest at ZT0.
source: A previous study in the rat prefrontal cortex found that synaptic elimination was highest at ZT0 (Choudhury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Choudhury et al., 2020.

claim: There may be brain region-specific pruning patterns by time of day.
source: While we did not examine ZT0, it is worth noting that these studies were done in the prefrontal cortex suggesting potential brain region-specific pruning patterns by time of day.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different brain regions may show different patterns of time-of-day variation in synaptic pruning.

claim: Heterogeneity in synaptic pruning has been described, with areas such as the cerebellum exhibiting greater microglial phagocytic capacity.
source: Heterogeneity in synaptic pruning has already been described, with areas such as the cerebellum exhibiting greater microglial phagocytic capacity (Ayata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Ayata et al., 2018.

claim: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases have been linked to circadian disruption.
source: This work has clear implications for neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases, which have been linked to circadian disruption as well as complement dysregulation and synapse loss.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on previous literature.

claim: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases have been linked to complement dysregulation and synapse loss.
source: This work has clear implications for neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases, which have been linked to circadian disruption as well as complement dysregulation and synapse loss.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on previous literature.

claim: REV-ERBα is a nuclear receptor with available small-molecule ligands.
source: Since REV-ERBα is a nuclear receptor with available small-molecule ligands (Solt et al., 2012), our findings suggest that it could be a therapeutic target for neurological and psychiatric disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Solt et al., 2012.

claim: REV-ERBα could be a therapeutic target for neurological and psychiatric disease.
source: Since REV-ERBα is a nuclear receptor with available small-molecule ligands (Solt et al., 2012), our findings suggest that it could be a therapeutic target for neurological and psychiatric disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that REV-ERBα regulates complement expression and synaptic phagocytosis, processes relevant to disease.

claim: Activation of REV-ERBs appears to suppress microglial cytokine production.
source: In previous studies in the brain, activation of REV-ERBs appears to suppress microglial cytokine production (Griffin et al., 2019) while inhibition of REV-ERBs can induce microglial amyloid-beta uptake and decrease plaque burden in mice (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibition of REV-ERBs can induce microglial amyloid-beta uptake and decrease plaque burden in mice.
source: In previous studies in the brain, activation of REV-ERBs appears to suppress microglial cytokine production (Griffin et al., 2019) while inhibition of REV-ERBs can induce microglial amyloid-beta uptake and decrease plaque burden in mice (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Effects on synaptic engulfment should be considered as REV-ERB-based therapeutics are developed.
source: Effects on synaptic engulfment should be considered as REV-ERB-based therapeutics are developed.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the current study.
